Formalizes Conclusion object C_n=(P,Γ,R,κ,Σ,Π,t) (proposition, premises/evidence, inference rule, inference method, epistemic assessment, provenance, derivation time), letting KnowledgeOS answer 'why did you reach this conclusion?' not just 'what did you conclude?'.

lineage_claims_b_to_a.quote: Our Knowledge Atom is actually an Assertion, not a Proposition.

cross_group_lineage_claims.quote: Our Knowledge Atom is actually an Assertion, not a Proposition.

a_rows_sample.anchor: At least the following relations must be separated: = representation/structural equality; ≡ semantic equality; ≈ observational equivalence; ≅_I identity equivalence; ≅_P provenance-sensitive equivalence; ≅_H historical equivalence.
a_rows_sample.statement: The overloaded notation K1=K2 is decomposed into (at least) six distinct relations that must not be conflated: structural equality (=), semantic equality (equiv), observational equivalence (approx), identity equivalence (cong_I), provenance-sensitive equivalence (cong_P), and historical equivalence (cong_H); the corpus is said to explicitly record the first four distinctions and warn they are not interchangeable.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Same proposition ⇏ Same evidence identity. ... two observations can concern the same proposition while remaining distinct evidence objects.
a_rows_sample.statement: Preserved historical result: identity is not equality — two evidence objects e1,e2 can both support the same proposition p (Supports(e1,p) and Supports(e2,p)) without e1=e2; this affects provenance, deduplication, replay, validation, audit and merge, and is attributed to an earlier corpus reconstruction rather than newly derived here.

a_rows_sample.anchor: x =_str y iff their representations are structurally identical. ... =_str ≠ semantic equality unless the representation has already been proven canonical.
a_rows_sample.statement: Structural equality x=_str y (representations structurally identical) is computationally convenient but is warned to not equal semantic equality unless the representation is already proven canonical — two structurally different representations can denote the same semantic state.

a_rows_sample.anchor: x ≡_sem y iff Semantics(x)=Semantics(y). ... Semantic equality is conceptually appropriate, but currently underdefined.
a_rows_sample.statement: Semantic equality x equiv_sem y is defined via a semantic interpretation function Sem:Representation->Meaning being equal on x and y, but is flagged as not computationally decidable while Sem itself remains formally undefined — conceptually appropriate but currently underdefined.

a_rows_sample.anchor: H1 ≈ H2 iff every permitted observation produces the same result: ∀O∈𝒪: O(H1)=O(H2). ... This is the relation already underlying Step 260's behavioral quotient.
a_rows_sample.statement: Observational equivalence for histories (H1 approx H2 iff every permitted observation O produces the same result) and for states (K1 approx K2 iff every permitted state observation agrees) is identified as the same relation already underlying Step 260's behavioral quotient; notably it does not require internal representations to be identical.

a_rows_sample.anchor: SameId(x,y) ... Identity tracks denotation; equality compares values. This formulation is a reconstruction, not yet a corpus-proven final definition.
a_rows_sample.statement: Identity (SameId(x,y)) answers whether two references denote the same domain object, independent of value equality: x=_str y can hold with SameId false (two separately created records with identical content but distinct observations), and SameId can hold while representations differ (the same domain object having evolved) — 'identity tracks denotation; equality compares values', explicitly flagged as a reconstruction, not a corpus-proven final definition.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Historical equality asks: Are these states the same point or condition in an evolution history? ... Semantic equality ⇏ Historical equality.
a_rows_sample.statement: Historical equality asks whether two states are the same point in an evolution history, distinct from current semantic equality: K0 -Revise-> K1 can have K0 equiv_sem K1 (representation changed, semantics didn't) while K0 !=_H K1 (distinct historical states) — semantic equality does not imply historical equality; matters especially for Replay and audit.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Provenance is semantically relevant: K1 ≢ K2. Provenance is metadata only: K1 ≡ K2. ... equality cannot be resolved until the theory determines which information is semantically essential. This is a key dependency for Step 265.
a_rows_sample.statement: Provenance equality is genuinely ambiguous: given K1={p,e1}, K2={p,e2} with e1!=e2 both supporting p, either provenance is semantically relevant (K1 not-equiv K2) or metadata only (K1 equiv K2); the earlier corpus is said to identify this ambiguity explicitly and conclude it cannot be resolved until the theory determines which information is semantically essential — flagged as a key dependency for Step 265 (provenance placement).

a_rows_sample.anchor: No universal equality hierarchy has yet been proven. ... Identity and Provenance equality are independent dimensions.
a_rows_sample.statement: A candidate implication chain (structural => semantic => observational equivalence) is proposed but explicitly not declared universally valid without further assumptions; identity and provenance equality are treated as independent dimensions from this chain; current position: no universal equality hierarchy has yet been proven.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Explicit assertion membership ≠ semantic entailment. ... a∈_exp K ... K⊨a ... Stored fact ≠ logically derived fact.
a_rows_sample.statement: Membership in an assertion-based state K is typed into explicit assertion membership (a in_exp K, a is literally one of K's stored assertions) versus semantic consequence (K models a, semantically entailed but not necessarily stored) — a proposed formal distinction (not yet a theorem) preventing the category error of treating a stored fact as identical to a logically derived one; flagged as essential for Step 262's assertion type.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Merge equality: semantic + identity + provenance dependent. Exact final semantics remain unresolved.
a_rows_sample.statement: Operation test — Merge: Merge(K1,K2) cannot be specified using structural equality alone, since a1=(p,e1) and a2=(p,e2) sharing proposition p could legitimately merge to {a1,a2} (kept separate) or to a single combined-evidence assertion depending on ontology; Merge equality is semantic+identity+provenance dependent, with exact final semantics unresolved.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Supersession requires identity/version distinction. ... collapsing them under semantic equality would destroy the very relation x2 ≻ x1.
a_rows_sample.statement: Operation test — Supersede: if Meaning(x1)=Meaning(x2) but Identity(x1)!=Identity(x2) and x2 supersedes x1, collapsing x1,x2 under semantic equality would destroy the supersession relation x2 succ x1 itself; supersession therefore requires an identity/version distinction, strongly suggesting semantic equality alone cannot serve as the sole equality relation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Replay requires historical identity/equality independent of current state equality. ... Replay(H1)=K and Replay(H2)=K yet H1 ≠_H H2.
a_rows_sample.statement: Operation test — Replay: two distinct histories H1,H2 (H1 !=_H H2) can replay to the same current state K (Replay(H1)=Replay(H2)=K); Replay is treated by the corpus as a history/audit operation rather than another state transformation, and requires historical identity/equality independent of current-state equality.

a_rows_sample.anchor: | Operation | Structural equality | Semantic equality | Identity | Historical equality | Provenance | Current assessment | Merge...Supersede...Replay...Remove...Revise...Deduplicate...Validate
a_rows_sample.statement: The full operation/equality matrix across Merge, Supersede, Replay, Remove, Revise, Deduplicate, Validate rates each of structural/semantic/identity/historical/provenance equality as insufficient, required, relevant, potentially-required, or context-dependent per operation, with every row's overall status UNRESOLVED, NORMATIVE/DOMAIN-DEPENDENT (Deduplicate), or 'Assessment relation' (Validate); Remove requires identity for correct object targeting (must not remove a2 when removing a1 despite structural identity), Revise cannot use semantic equality as its sole target selector (must not implicitly revise x2 when revising x1 despite x1 equiv_sem x2), Deduplicate cannot be specified until its preservation policy is known (structural/semantic/identity/provenance criteria can each give different results), and Validate shows semantic state equality does not imply identical validation results because validation is a relation over (K,E) pairs, not K alone — reinforcing that not every operation is a state transformation T:K->K.

a_rows_sample.anchor: No single equality relation is adequate for all KnowledgeOS operations. ... KnowledgeOS requires a typed family of relations.
a_rows_sample.statement: Major correction to the kernel concept: rejects the implicit assumption 'KnowledgeOS needs one equality operator', replacing it with 'KnowledgeOS requires a typed family of relations' (=_str, equiv_sem, approx_obs, SameId, equiv_H, equiv_P) that may be connected by formally established implications but must not be conflated.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K1 ≡_K K2 ⟺ ∀O∈𝒪_K: O(K1)=O(K2) ... 𝒪_K is not yet completely closed. Therefore this is a candidate formal definition, not a completed theorem.
a_rows_sample.statement: Candidate formal definition of Knowledge-State equality as purely observational/behavioral: K1 equiv_K K2 iff every permitted state observation O in the (not-yet-closed) set O_K agrees on K1 and K2; explicitly a candidate, not a completed theorem, because O_K is not yet closed.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Equality → Congruence → Quotient → Minimality. This is the correct dependency direction.
a_rows_sample.statement: If K1 equiv_K K2 (no permitted observation distinguishes them) and all mandatory operations preserve that equivalence, equiv_K becomes the congruence relation needed for the minimal quotient K*=H/equiv (Step 260) — establishing the dependency direction Equality -> Congruence -> Quotient -> Minimality as correct.

a_rows_sample.anchor: the observation set is not fully closed; the operation registry is not fully closed; provenance placement remains unresolved; assertion semantics remain unresolved; temporal semantics remain unresolved; identity semantics remain unresolved. The governing prompt explicitly says that final kernel sele
a_rows_sample.statement: Explicit refusal to overclaim equiv_K as final: six named open dependencies remain (observation-set closure, operation-registry closure, provenance placement, assertion semantics, temporal semantics, identity semantics); the governing prompt is cited as requiring final kernel selection to halt while equality remains ambiguous, and this gate is obeyed.

a_rows_sample.anchor: bounded contexts may legitimately require different relations: same assertion / same evidence / same domain identity / same version / same semantic meaning / same observable state ... PRIMARY KEY must therefore not automatically be interpreted as SemanticIdentity. ... content hash must not automatic
a_rows_sample.statement: DDD interpretation: rather than one generic 'Equality' concept used everywhere, different bounded contexts legitimately require different named relations (same assertion, same evidence, same domain identity, same version, same semantic meaning, same observable state); a database PRIMARY KEY must not automatically be interpreted as SemanticIdentity, and a content hash must not automatically become DomainIdentity.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 𝔎=(K,=_str,≡_sem,≈_obs,SameId,≡_H,≡_P). The next question is not 'Which one is the equality?' It is 'Which relation is the appropriate congruence relation for each operation and which relation defines semantic equality of Knowledge States?'
a_rows_sample.statement: Mathematical reframing: KnowledgeOS's state carries a relational structure 𝔎=(K,=_str,equiv_sem,approx_obs,SameId,equiv_H,equiv_P) rather than a single equality; the research question shifts from 'which relation is THE equality' to 'which relation is the appropriate congruence for each operation, and which defines semantic equality of Knowledge States'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The governing criterion is: F_i(H_1)=F_i(H_2) must imply F_i(\widehat T(H_1,c)) = F_i(\widehat T(H_2,c))
b_rows_sample.statement: A candidate Knowledge-State abstraction F_i:H->K_i is sufficient for a mandatory transformation T over admissible context c iff F_i(H1)=F_i(H2) implies F_i(That(H1,c))=F_i(That(H2,c)); strengthened to require an actual state-level transformation T_i:K_i x C -> K_i such that F_i(That(H,c)) = T_i(F_i(H),c) for all admissible H,c (a commuting square between history-level and state-level transformations).

b_rows_sample.anchor: In particular: Definition of K != Adequacy of K, and: Congruence criterion valid != KnowledgeOS satisfies congruence.
b_rows_sample.statement: Self-correction of the immediately preceding step: a mathematical definition of K, a candidate representation of K, an abstraction F:H->K, and the claim that F is sufficient for the transformation family are four distinct claims that must not be conflated; Step 258 wrongly treated K as already a well-defined state abstraction.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Not every operation has the form: T:K -> K. ... Assess:K x X -> Assessment ... Authorize:Actor x Action x Policy -> Decision
b_rows_sample.statement: Operations must first be classified into (1) knowledge-state transformations, (2) epistemic assessments, (3) governance operations, (4) audit/history operations, (5) observation operations; not every legitimate KnowledgeOS operation is an endomorphism T:K->K — e.g. Assess:K x X -> Assessment and Authorize:Actor x Action x Policy -> Decision are non-state-closing operations, and only state-transforming operations enter the primary congruence test.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Now introduce a revision rule dependent on lineage: Revise(x_1,x_2) is permitted only if: Origin(x_1) in ApprovedSources.
b_rows_sample.statement: Conditional counterexample sketch for candidate F_A (artifact-set state) under Revise: if revision eligibility depends on Origin(x1) (an approved-sources lineage rule) while F_A discards origin, two histories with equal F_A images can differ in whether a subsequent Revise is valid, which would falsify F_A's congruence — but this is CONDITIONAL, not PROVEN, unless the corpus actually establishes that revision eligibility depends on origin.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Merge is the strongest initial discriminator ... If the resulting provenance must distinguish Source_1 from Source_2, then F_A(\widehat{Merge}(H_A)) != F_A(\widehat{Merge}(H_B)).
b_rows_sample.statement: Conditional counterexample sketch for candidate F_A under Merge, described as the strongest initial discriminator among the tested operations: if two histories reach the same artifact x1 from different sources (Source_1 vs Source_2) with F_A(H_A)=F_A(H_B)={x1}, and a subsequent Merge(x1,x2) must record provenance distinguishing Source_1 from Source_2, then F_A fails congruence — again only if provenance is established as semantically observable by Merge, which the governing prompt requires testing (alongside evidence, replay, validation, implementation needs) before deciding whether Evidence/provenance belongs inside or outside K.

b_rows_sample.anchor: All transformations are K -> K | REFUTED as a universal assumption
b_rows_sample.statement: The results table explicitly marks the assumption that all KnowledgeOS transformations have signature K->K as REFUTED as a universal assumption (distinguished from the still-CANDIDATE status of F:H->K as a useful abstraction model, and from several UNRESOLVED items: whether history can be discarded, whether provenance must be inside or can remain outside K, whether the transformation family is closed, whether current K is globally sufficient, whether a minimal K exists).

b_rows_sample.anchor: We cannot perform a valid global congruence proof until the mandatory transformation family is itself sufficiently closed. ... the quantifier forall T in T has no determinate meaning if T is incomplete.
b_rows_sample.statement: Central negative result of the step: a valid global congruence proof is impossible while the mandatory transformation family T is not itself closed, because the universal quantifier 'for all T in T' is not well-defined over an incomplete set; this reinforces the required sequencing Transformation Inventory -> Semantic Classification -> Congruence, rather than jumping to K -> Congruence in isolation.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A finite test set can establish: Congruent_{tested}(F). It does not automatically establish: Congruent_{global}(F).
b_rows_sample.statement: Local/tested congruence (survival of a finite, executed test set) must be distinguished from global congruence (a formal proof over the fully specified domain and transformation family); an executed test yields only 'evidence of survival', never 'proof of universal congruence'.

b_rows_sample.anchor: This also explains why Step 260 must come after Step 259. Minimality asks whether K* is the coarsest sufficient abstraction. But we cannot establish sufficiency until we know which operations must be preserved.
b_rows_sample.statement: Sequencing principle: no valid minimality proof (Step 260, testing whether K* = H/equiv is the coarsest sufficient state abstraction) can precede the operation registry and congruence-matrix analysis (Step 259), since minimality presupposes knowledge of which operations a sufficient state must preserve.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A bounded context state is legitimate only if its externally observable behavior does not depend on information that the context has discarded. ... K1 equiv_K K2 must imply identical behavior under the context's published operations.
b_rows_sample.statement: DDD interpretation of the congruence criterion: a bounded-context state representation is legitimate only when its externally observable behavior under the context's published operations does not depend on information the context's state has discarded — i.e. the congruence test is a rigorous check for an accidentally omitted domain invariant, not mathematical decoration.

b_rows_sample.anchor: We must not assume: Statistical Sufficiency => KnowledgeOS Operational Sufficiency. That requires proof.
b_rows_sample.statement: Statistical interpretation: two histories can produce the same estimated distribution P_theta under a distributional candidate state F_E, yet still be distinguishable by a future transformation dependent on information not identifiable from that distribution; statistical sufficiency must not be assumed to imply KnowledgeOS operational sufficiency without separate proof.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Step 259 establishes the formal mechanism by which candidate Knowledge-State abstractions can be falsified, but it does not yet establish that any candidate abstraction is globally sufficient. ... if the quotient does not exist in the required usable form, that is a valid research result.
b_rows_sample.statement: Conservative step verdict: the congruence-falsification mechanism is established but no candidate is proven globally sufficient; Step 260 is set up to test — not assume — existence, uniqueness, representability, computability, decidability, composability, equality, membership and identity of the candidate minimal quotient K*=H/equiv (H1 equiv H2 iff no mandatory operation can distinguish them), explicitly allowing a negative result (the quotient not existing in usable form) as a valid outcome.

b_rows_sample.anchor: H1 ≈ H2 iff every permitted observation produces the same result: ∀O∈𝒪: O(H1)=O(H2). ... This is the relation already underlying Step 260's behavioral quotient.
b_rows_sample.statement: Observational equivalence for histories (H1 approx H2 iff every permitted observation O produces the same result) and for states (K1 approx K2 iff every permitted state observation agrees) is identified as the same relation already underlying Step 260's behavioral quotient; notably it does not require internal representations to be identical.

b_rows_sample.anchor: K1 ≡_K K2 ⟺ ∀O∈𝒪_K: O(K1)=O(K2) ... 𝒪_K is not yet completely closed. Therefore this is a candidate formal definition, not a completed theorem.
b_rows_sample.statement: Candidate formal definition of Knowledge-State equality as purely observational/behavioral: K1 equiv_K K2 iff every permitted state observation O in the (not-yet-closed) set O_K agrees on K1 and K2; explicitly a candidate, not a completed theorem, because O_K is not yet closed.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Equality → Congruence → Quotient → Minimality. This is the correct dependency direction.
b_rows_sample.statement: If K1 equiv_K K2 (no permitted observation distinguishes them) and all mandatory operations preserve that equivalence, equiv_K becomes the congruence relation needed for the minimal quotient K*=H/equiv (Step 260) — establishing the dependency direction Equality -> Congruence -> Quotient -> Minimality as correct.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Transformation-sufficiency test F(H1) = F(H2) ⇒ F(T(H1,i)) = F(T(H2,i)) — executed, congruent for every input tested. See artifact F.
b_rows_sample.statement: The transformation-sufficiency (congruence) test F(H1)=F(H2) => F(T(H1,i))=F(T(H2,i)) was executed and found congruent for every tested input, with full detail deferred to a separate artifact F — direct empirical support for the K=(A,R) abstraction passing the Step-259 congruence criterion.

b_rows_sample.anchor: The model is executable, so removal is testable. The phrase MINIMAL KERNEL is therefore earned — but only in the sense step 254 names: Minimality(K | 𝒯), relative to the transformation set. Not ontological necessity. A richer 𝒯 could force more.
b_rows_sample.statement: Minimality caveat: the removal-based necessity audit only earns Minimality(K|T) relative to the specific tested transformation set T (per step 254's framing), never ontological necessity of the components — a richer transformation set could force additional components to become necessary.

b_rows_sample.anchor: F(Hx) = F(Hy) ? False — different states, so congruence is NOT tested by this pair ... A congruence test requires two DIFFERENT histories producing the SAME state. Two of my first three attempts were vacuous, and would have "passed" while proving nothing.
b_rows_sample.statement: Self-disclosed methodological failure: two of the first three attempted congruence-test constructions used history pairs that already produced different F-images, meaning congruence was never actually being tested (a vacuous pass); a valid congruence test requires two DIFFERENT histories that fold to the SAME state F(H1)=F(H2).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Hr = [assert A1, assert A4] ; Hs = [assert A4, assert A1] ... F(Hr) = F(Hs) = True ... i = relate(A1,A4,supersedes) -> congruent: True ... i = assert A2 -> congruent: True ... i = relate(A4,A1,refines) -> congruent: True ... F(H1) = F(H3) where H3 re-asserts A1 (idempotence) -> congruent: True. No c
b_rows_sample.statement: Valid executed congruence test: order-reversed histories Hr=[assert A1, assert A4] and Hs=[assert A4, assert A1] satisfy the precondition F(Hr)=F(Hs); three different subsequent operations (relate-supersedes, assert, relate-refines) are each tested and found congruent, plus an idempotence test (re-asserting A1); no counterexample is found across these tests.

b_rows_sample.anchor: T's derived signature is 𝕂 × Op × Policy × Authority ⇀ 𝕂 × Outcome. History is not in its domain. A function cannot depend on an argument it does not receive. Congruence therefore holds by construction, under exactly two assumptions: A1 · T reads only K, Policy, Authority — PROVEN ... A2 · no operat
b_rows_sample.statement: Structural (by-construction) explanation for why congruence held in every test: T's derived signature K x Op x Policy x Authority -harpoon-> K x Outcome does not include History in its domain, so T cannot depend on it — a function cannot depend on an argument it does not receive. This holds under exactly two assumptions: A1 (T reads only K, Policy, Authority — PROVEN by elimination of actor/time/evidence/context during signature derivation) and A2 (no operation consults order-of-arrival — HOLDS for the twelve derived operations because A and R are sets, making order structurally unobservable).

a_notations: K1 equiv_K K2 iff forall O in O_K: O(K1)=O(K2)
b_notations: commuting square F o That = T_i o F

group_evidence.why_grouped: labels co-occur in the same contribution's labels[] 5 separate times across the corpus

a_rows_sample.anchor: After we separate the concerns of a knowledge system using DDD, where does 'sunya' appear as a property of the knowledge system? Knowledge Sunya may be the absence of inherent, context-independent determination. Not 'knowledge is nothing.' Rather: No knowledge claim is self-sufficiently determined o
a_rows_sample.statement: Poses the central question of where 'sunya' appears once a knowledge system's concerns are DDD-separated, answering that Knowledge Sunya is the absence of inherent, context-independent determination -- no knowledge claim is self-sufficiently determined outside the relations that give it meaning -- not that knowledge is nothing.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Question Context: What are we trying to determine? Claim Context: What is being asserted? Evidence Context: What supports or challenges the assertion? Challenge Context: What could invalidate, restrict, contradict or qualify it? Determination Context: What can currently be justified? Revision Contex
a_rows_sample.statement: Applies DDD separation of concerns to a knowledge system, defining six bounded contexts (Question, Claim, Evidence, Challenge, Determination, Revision) each with a distinct responsibility, preventing the conflation of claim, truth, evidence, determination, and knowledge into one object.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Status(C) != f(C) but rather: Status(C) = f(C, Q, Context, E, Standards, t). This is where I think Knowledge Sunya begins to appear.
a_rows_sample.statement: Formalizes that a claim's status is never a function of the claim alone (Status(C)!=f(C)) but of the claim together with question, context, evidence, standards, and time (Status(C)=f(C,Q,Context,E,Standards,t)), identifying this as the entry point where Knowledge Sunya begins to appear.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge Sunya does not mean Claim=empty-set. It means something more subtle: Claim not-equiv Knowledge and Claim not-equiv Determination. A claim by itself does not carry its complete epistemic status. It requires relations.
a_rows_sample.statement: Clarifies that Knowledge Sunya does not mean the claim object is empty, but rather that a claim is not equivalent to knowledge and not equivalent to determination -- a claim by itself does not carry its complete epistemic status, which requires relations to other contexts.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Claim \ Question. The claim still syntactically exists. But its epistemic determination may disappear. Claim \ Evidence. The assertion remains, but justification may disappear. Claim \ Context. Its applicability may disappear. Sunya may occur not in the object, but in the missing relation.
a_rows_sample.statement: Argues, via three worked removals (Claim minus Question, minus Evidence, minus Context), that Sunya occurs not in the object itself but in a missing relation: removing the question can erase epistemic determination, removing evidence can erase justification, and removing context can erase applicability, even though the claim syntactically persists.

a_rows_sample.anchor: KnowledgeSunya(C|Q,X,E,S,t) when the claim has no justified determination under the specified epistemic relations. KnowledgeSunya(C|Q,E,t) if not-exists d Determine(d,C,Q,E,t). But crucially KnowledgeSunya(C|Q,E,t) does not mean C=false, and does not mean C=nonexistent. It means: the epistemic syste
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines the research predicate KnowledgeSunya(C|Q,X,E,S,t): the claim has no justified determination under the specified epistemic relations (not-exists d such that Determine(d,C,Q,E,t)), explicitly not implying the claim is false or nonexistent, only that the epistemic system currently has no justified determination of it under that frame.

a_rows_sample.anchor: D(C1) != D(C2). The claim itself didn't change. Its relational determination changed. This is extremely close to our earlier finding with Zero: Zero(x|D1) != Zero(x|D2).
a_rows_sample.statement: Shows via a worked context-change example (the same claim C determined under context C1 but undetermined under context C2, D(C1)!=D(C2), with the claim itself unchanged) that relational determination is context-relative, drawing a direct parallel to the already-established contextual-Zero finding Zero(x|D1)!=Zero(x|D2).

a_rows_sample.anchor: 1. Object emptiness: X=empty-set. There is literally no object/content. 2. Determination emptiness: Determine(X,K_t)=empty-set. There is no justified determination. 3. Relational emptiness: Contribution(X|Q,C,E)=0. The object contributes nothing under a specified epistemic relation. These are not eq
a_rows_sample.statement: Fixes a Knowledge Sunya triangle of three explicitly non-equivalent emptiness notions: Object emptiness (X=empty-set), Determination emptiness (Determine(X,K_t)=empty-set), and Relational emptiness (Contribution(X|Q,C,E)=0) -- Object Sunya != Knowledge Sunya != Contribution Zero.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Evidence Context: 'supports' != Claim Context: 'asserts' != Determination Context: 'justified' != Governance Context: 'accepted' != Execution Context: 'authorized'. A piece of information can exist in one context while having no determination in another. Meaning is bounded by context. Sunya appears
a_rows_sample.statement: Argues that Sunya is a boundary concept between bounded contexts (Evidence's 'supports', Claim's 'asserts', Determination's 'justified', Governance's 'accepted', Execution's 'authorized' are all distinct meanings), since information existing in one context can have no determination in another -- meaning is bounded by context, and Sunya appears exactly where an assumed intrinsic meaning disappears once context boundaries are respected.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Evidence.supports(C) does not automatically imply Determination.justified(C). And Determination.justified(C) does not automatically imply Governance.accepted(C). And Governance.accepted(C) does not imply C=True, unless the relevant contract explicitly establishes that relationship. So every boundary
a_rows_sample.statement: Chains three explicit non-implications across bounded contexts (Evidence.supports does not imply Determination.justified; Determination.justified does not imply Governance.accepted; Governance.accepted does not imply True, absent an explicit contract), concluding every inter-context boundary creates a possible semantic emptiness: a relation not established implies no legitimate inference -- possibly the most useful KnowledgeOS interpretation of Sunya.

a_rows_sample.anchor: We should not say 'DDD proves Nagarjuna.' It does not. Madhyamaka gives us a philosophical hypothesis: things do not possess independent inherent existence; their determination depends upon relations. DDD gives us an architectural method: separate contexts according to different semantic responsibil
a_rows_sample.statement: Explicitly refuses to claim 'DDD proves Nagarjuna', instead assigning each tradition its proper role: Madhyamaka supplies a philosophical hypothesis (things lack independent inherent existence; determination depends on relations), DDD supplies an architectural method (separate contexts by semantic responsibility, never assume universal validity of one context's meaning), and KnowledgeOS supplies the actual epistemic research question (does context-relative determination produce meaningful epistemic emptiness when determining relations are removed).

a_rows_sample.anchor: K_t = (C_t, E_t, Ch_t, D_t, Q_t, R_t, H_t) where C_t=claims, E_t=evidence, Ch_t=challenges, D_t=determinations, Q_t=questions, R_t=revisions, H_t=history/provenance. Knowledge Sunya could occur when a required relational path to determination is absent: C_t -?-> D_t. There is a claim. But no valid p
a_rows_sample.statement: Restructures the knowledge state K_t into seven explicit relational components (claims, evidence, challenges, determinations, questions, revisions, history/provenance), locating Knowledge Sunya as the absence of a required relational path from claims to determination (C_t != empty-set while D_t(C_t)=empty-set), a very different kind of emptiness from an empty claim set.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K_t: C='X always causes Y.' Challenge: counterexample. Determine_t(C)=Universal becomes Determine_{t+1}(C)=Conditional. The previous determination becomes empty with respect to the universal claim, but not empty with respect to the qualified claim. Universal(C) -> Sunya -> Conditional(C). Sunya can
a_rows_sample.statement: Illustrates Sunya as a transitional epistemic space via a worked example: a universal claim challenged by a counterexample transitions Universal(C)->Sunya->Conditional(C), where the prior universal determination becomes empty while a qualified determination has not yet been established -- not 'there is nothing' but a state between two determinations.

a_rows_sample.anchor: Determination -> Challenge -> Sunya -> Revision -> New Determination. The negative contribution can create a temporary epistemic Sunya from which a better determination emerges. ... Argument -> Challenge -> Sunya -> Qualification -> Purified Knowledge. The challenge removes the false certainty, not
a_rows_sample.statement: Inserts Sunya into the purification cycle as an intermediate transitional stage (Determination->Challenge->Sunya->Revision->New Determination, equivalently Argument->Challenge->Sunya->Qualification->Purified Knowledge), proposing the candidate interpretation that Knowledge Sunya is not the absence of knowledge but the absence of unjustified determination -- the challenge removes false certainty, not the underlying subject matter -- kept as a candidate interpretation pending testing.

a_rows_sample.anchor: H-SUNYA-01 -- Relational Epistemic Emptiness. A knowledge claim has no inherent epistemic determination independent of the question, context, evidence, standards and temporal state through which it is evaluated. ... Empty_{Q,C,E,S}(x,K_t) iff not-exists d Determine(d|x,Q,C,E,S,K_t), while explicitly
a_rows_sample.statement: States the formal research hypothesis H-SUNYA-01 (Relational Epistemic Emptiness): a knowledge claim has no inherent epistemic determination independent of question, context, evidence, standards, and time, formalized as Empty_{Q,C,E,S}(x,K_t) iff no determination exists under those relations, with the two required non-implications explicitly preserved (never implies the claim is false, never implies the claim is the empty object).

a_rows_sample.anchor: Elimination Zero: representation. Balance Zero: contribution. Knowledge Sunya: determination. Purification: transition. They interact, but we don't yet know whether they are manifestations of one deeper mathematical structure. That should be discovered, not assumed.
a_rows_sample.statement: Consolidates the four Zero-adjacent research threads by their domain -- Elimination Zero (representation), Balance Zero (contribution), Knowledge Sunya (determination), Purification (transition) -- explicitly leaving open, as a discovery question rather than an assumption, whether they are manifestations of one deeper mathematical structure.

a_rows_sample.anchor: K_t --challenge--> Sunya --inquiry--> K_{t+1} may become the epistemic purification cycle. Knowledge Sunya is not 'nothingness in knowledge'; it is the state in which a determination has no valid grounding within a specified epistemic frame. And DDD gives us the machinery to locate which relation is
a_rows_sample.statement: States the strongest current hypothesis and closing architecture: K_t--challenge-->Sunya--inquiry-->K_{t+1} as the epistemic purification cycle, with Knowledge Sunya defined as the state in which a determination has no valid grounding within a specified epistemic frame, observable precisely at the DDD boundary where a claim's assumed inherent determination disappears once its supporting relations are separated and made explicit.

b_rows_sample.anchor: K_{t+1} = Pres(K_t) + Rev(K_t) + New(K_t) - Rejected(K_t). The critical question becomes: What is the status of what has been removed? Is it zero? No -- not necessarily.
b_rows_sample.statement: Replaces the naive additive knowledge-transition model K_{t+1}=K_t+DeltaK with a richer decomposition K_{t+1}=Pres(K_t)+Rev(K_t)+New(K_t)-Rejected(K_t), posing the critical open question of what status the rejected/removed portion actually has -- explicitly not assumed to be zero.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Asti (exists), Nasti (does not exist), Ubhaya (both), Nobhayam (neither). The important conceptual move is that Sunya is not simply the fourth object 'nothing.' ... absence from knowledge != non-existence. [Causes of absence: rejected, superseded, unresolved, irrelevant, redundant, outside the curre
b_rows_sample.statement: Reads Nagarjuna's four alternatives (Asti/Nasti/Ubhaya/Nobhayam) as showing Sunya is not simply the fourth alternative 'nothing', extracting the KnowledgeOS principle that absence from knowledge is not non-existence, since a proposition's absence from K_{t+1} can have at least nine distinct causes (rejected, superseded, unresolved, irrelevant, redundant, outside the current question, deliberately abstracted away, contradicted, never established).

b_rows_sample.anchor: K_t = P_t union R_t union E_t where P_t=preserved knowledge, R_t=revised/transformed knowledge, E_t=eliminated/removed content. Then ask: What is E_t? This is where emptiness might enter.
b_rows_sample.statement: Partitions a knowledge-transition step into preserved (P_t), revised (R_t), and eliminated (E_t) content, posing the question of what E_t actually is as the entry point for the emptiness discussion.

b_rows_sample.anchor: A. Representational emptiness: R(x)=empty set, ordinary absence. B. Epistemic emptiness: Determine(x,K_t)=empty set. This does not mean x does not exist. It means knowledge has no justified determination of x. C. Relational emptiness: Pi(T(D))=Pi(T(D\x)). That is precisely our existing Transformatio
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes three kinds of emptiness -- Representational (ordinary absence, R(x)=empty set), Epistemic (no justified determination, Determine(x,K_t)=empty set, not implying x does not exist), and Relational (the pre-existing Transformation-relative Zero, Pi(T(D))=Pi(T(D\x))) -- concluding Zero_{T,Pi}(x;D) is neither x=empty-set nor x=false.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Zero_{T,Pi}(x;K_t) but after a challenge or new evidence: not Zero_{T,Pi}(x;K_{t+1}). Then Zero is clearly state-relative and time-relative: Zero_t(x) != Zero_{t+1}(x). ... consistent with what our experiments already suggested about contextual Zero.
b_rows_sample.statement: Time-indexes the existing Zero definition (Zero_{T,Pi}(x;K_t) vs Zero_{T,Pi}(x;K_{t+1})), demonstrating Zero is both state-relative and time-relative (Zero_t(x) != Zero_{t+1}(x)), consistent with and extending the already-established contextual-Zero finding that an element can be eliminable in one context and not in another.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Perhaps some knowledge-state questions cannot be represented adequately by a binary present/absent state. Status_t(x) in {Established, Rejected, Unresolved, Qualified}. Or perhaps, more fundamentally, Status_t(x|Q,C,E). The status is relative to question Q, context C, evidence E, time t.
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes replacing a binary present/absent knowledge-state representation with a richer status typing Status_t(x) in {Established, Rejected, Unresolved, Qualified}, or more fundamentally Status_t(x|Q,C,E) relative to question, context, evidence, and time.

b_rows_sample.anchor: K_t: 'X is always true.' Challenge discovers an exception. K_{t+1}: 'X is true under conditions C.' We lost information, in one sense: scope(K_{t+1})<scope(K_t). But we may have gained epistemic quality: Validity(K_{t+1})>Validity(K_t). So the removed part is not simply 'negative knowledge.' It is u
b_rows_sample.statement: Illustrates K_t->K_{t+1} as a purification process with a worked example: a universal claim 'X is always true' becomes the qualified 'X is true under conditions C' after a challenge, so scope decreases (scope(K_{t+1})<scope(K_t)) while validity increases (Validity(K_{t+1})>Validity(K_t)), with the removed part being unsupported structure, not negative knowledge.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Knowledge Difference != Knowledge Loss. Knowledge Reduction != Epistemic Degradation. A transition can reduce representation while preserving the question (D->R) or reduce claim scope while improving epistemic validity (K_t->K_{t+1}). These are two completely different reduction processes.
b_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes Knowledge Difference from Knowledge Loss and Knowledge Reduction from Epistemic Degradation, noting representation reduction (D->R, preserving the question) and knowledge-state reduction (K_t->K_{t+1}, improving validity while shrinking scope) are two completely different reduction processes that must not be conflated.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Loss_t = K_t \ K_{t+1}. But some x in Loss_t may have different statuses: Rejected_t, Superseded_t, Redundant_t, Unresolved_t, Irrelevant_t, Purified_t. So the space between K_t and K_{t+1} is not necessarily empty. It may contain epistemic transition structure. K_t --tau_t--> (K_{t+1}, Delta_t, Gam
b_rows_sample.statement: Investigates a 'knowledge vacuum' hypothesis: the loss set Loss_t=K_t\K_{t+1} may partition into six distinct statuses (Rejected, Superseded, Redundant, Unresolved, Irrelevant, Purified), so the space between K_t and K_{t+1} contains epistemic transition structure rather than being empty, formalized as K_t--tau_t-->(K_{t+1}, Delta_t, Gamma_t) carrying both the change and its justification.

b_rows_sample.anchor: KA_T = (K, T, Delta, Gamma, equiv, Pi) where K=knowledge states, T=admissible transformations, Delta=state difference/residue, Gamma=justification of transition, equiv=epistemic equivalence, Pi=observations/contractions. Can transitions compose? Is there an identity transition I(K)=K? Are there inve
b_rows_sample.statement: Proposes a candidate knowledge transition algebra KA_T=(K,T,Delta,Gamma,equiv,Pi) (knowledge states, admissible transformations, state residue, transition justification, epistemic equivalence, observations) rather than beginning with (K,+), posing four experimental questions: whether transitions compose, whether an identity transition exists, whether inverse transitions exist (probably not, since knowledge revision is usually not reversible), and whether purification is idempotent (P(P(K))=P(K), potentially yielding P^2=P as an experimentally supported property).

b_rows_sample.anchor: I would not currently write Sunyata=Zero. That would collapse very different concepts. Instead: Sunyata leads to research inspiration for relational non-substantiality, while our formal Zero remains Zero_{T,Pi}(x;D). Empty_{Q,C}(K_t) meaning: Under question Q and contract/context C, the current know
b_rows_sample.statement: Explicitly refuses to write Sunyata=Zero (which would collapse distinct concepts), positioning Sunyata only as research inspiration for relational non-substantiality while the formal Zero_{T,Pi}(x;D) remains unchanged, and introduces a new predicate Empty_{Q,C}(K_t) (the current knowledge state contains no justified determination relevant to Q) that does not imply K_t is the empty set -- a knowledge state can be enormous while empty with respect to one particular question.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Elimination Zero / Balance Zero / Epistemic Emptiness, corresponding to representation / contribution / knowledge state, connected by time K_t --challenge/evidence/revision--> K_{t+1}. Knowledge Algebra is fundamentally an algebra of transitions and preserved/revised relations, not an algebra of sta
b_rows_sample.statement: Identifies a research triangle of three Zero-adjacent notions -- Elimination Zero (representation), Balance Zero (contribution), and Epistemic Emptiness (knowledge state) -- connected by the temporal transition K_t->K_{t+1}, proposing as a hypothesis (not conclusion) that Knowledge Algebra is fundamentally an algebra of transitions and preserved/revised relations, not an algebra of static knowledge objects.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Do not identify what is absent from a representation or determination with what does not exist. Epistemic absence != ontological non-existence. And an even stronger one: A zero result is always zero relative to a specified state, transformation, question, and observation.
b_rows_sample.statement: Turns Nagarjuna's warning into two KnowledgeOS research principles: epistemic absence is not ontological non-existence, and a zero result is always zero relative to a specified state, transformation, question, and observation -- consistent with the direction the Zero experiments have already forced.

b_rows_sample.anchor: KR-STATE-TRANSITION-01 -- Knowledge State, Emptiness and Purification, testing whether K_t -> K_{t+1} can empirically distinguish removed, rejected, unresolved, redundant, purified, and question-empty states without conflating them.
b_rows_sample.statement: Commissions experiment KR-STATE-TRANSITION-01 (Knowledge State, Emptiness and Purification) to test whether a knowledge-state transition K_t->K_{t+1} can empirically distinguish removed, rejected, unresolved, redundant, purified, and question-empty states without collapsing them into one generic category.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Epistemic Absence != Ontological Non-Existence: Determine(x,K_t)=empty-set does NOT imply x=false or x=non-existent. Knowledge Difference != Epistemic Degradation: scope(K_{t+1})<scope(K_t) often yields Validity(K_{t+1})>Validity(K_t); scope reduction under challenge is the formal mechanism of Purif
b_rows_sample.statement: Consolidates three key epistemic principles with formal signatures: Epistemic Absence != Ontological Non-Existence (Determine(x,K_t)=empty-set does not entail falsity or non-existence), Knowledge Difference != Epistemic Degradation (scope reduction under challenge is the formal mechanism of Purification, since scope can shrink while validity rises), and an 'Epistemic Triad of Zero' table mapping Representation/Elimination-Zero, Contribution/Balance-Zero, and Knowledge-State/Epistemic-Emptiness each to a precise formal signature.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Delta_t in {Rejected_t, Superseded_t, Redundant_t, Unresolved_t, Irrelevant_t, Purified_t}. Idempotency of Purification: P(P(K_t)) equiv_Q P(K_t) => P^2=P, once a knowledge state is purified relative to challenge set Gamma, applying the same purification transformation yields no further reduction. N
b_rows_sample.statement: Finalizes three formal candidate properties for empirical verification: idempotency of purification (P(P(K_t)) equiv_Q P(K_t), giving P^2=P once a challenge-relative purification stabilizes), non-reversibility of revision (tau^{-1}(K_{t+1}) != K_t in general, due to loss of unrectified assumptions), and question-relative emptiness invariance (Empty_Q(K_t) never implies K_t is the empty set).

b_rows_sample.anchor: KR-STATE-TRANSITION-01 primary objectives: 1. Status Discrimination: verify KnowledgeOS engines can programmatically distinguish Rejected, Superseded, Redundant, Unresolved, and Purified states without collapsing them into a generic null/false/deleted state. 2. Purification Stability: experimentally
b_rows_sample.statement: Specifies three primary objectives for KR-STATE-TRANSITION-01: status discrimination (programmatically distinguishing Rejected/Superseded/Redundant/Unresolved/Purified states without collapsing them into a generic null/false/deleted category), purification stability (testing convergence of challenge-driven revision sequences to an idempotent state P^2=P), and differential tracking (validating that retaining the transition residue (Delta_t,Gamma_t) prevents information loss during non-monotonic updates).

b_rows_sample.anchor: Delta_t = K_t \ K_{t+1}. That captures removal, but not transformation. 'X is always true' becomes 'X is true under C'. The original claim has not simply disappeared. It has been qualified. Therefore: Delta_t = (Delta_t^-, Delta_t^o, Delta_t^+) where Delta_t^- = removed/rejected/superseded, Delta_t^
b_rows_sample.statement: Corrects the residue definition from plain set difference Delta_t=K_t\K_{t+1} (which only captures removal) to a tripartite residue Delta_t=(Delta_t^-,Delta_t^o,Delta_t^+) covering removed/rejected/superseded, transformed/qualified, and newly acquired material, since a claim like 'X is always true' becoming 'X is true under C' is qualification, not disappearance.

b_rows_sample.anchor: Residue(tau_t,K_t,K_{t+1}) because two transitions can produce the same final state while having completely different histories. ... a claim was falsified; superseded; evidence was withdrawn; a redundant representation was removed; a claim was narrowed through qualification. Same endpoint. Different
b_rows_sample.statement: Establishes that the residue can be more important than the endpoint difference: since multiple distinct epistemic histories (falsification, supersession, evidence withdrawal, redundancy removal, qualification) can all produce the same final state K_{t+1}, the endpoint state alone does not fully characterize the epistemic state transition.

b_rows_sample.anchor: K_t = empty-set: knowledge-state emptiness. Empty_Q(K_t): question-relative epistemic emptiness. Zero_{T,Pi}(x;D): transformation-relative eliminability. These should remain separate. Empty_{Q,C}(K_t) means: not-exists d [Determine(d,Q,C,K_t)]. But this does not imply K_t=empty-set. And it certainly
b_rows_sample.statement: Fixes a three-level distinction that must remain separate: knowledge-state emptiness (K_t=empty-set), question-relative epistemic emptiness (Empty_{Q,C}(K_t), formally not-exists d such that Determine(d,Q,C,K_t)), and transformation-relative eliminability (Zero_{T,Pi}(x;D)) -- Empty_{Q,C}(K_t) implies neither K_t=empty-set nor that Q itself has no answer.

a_aliases: Where Sunya appears after DDD separation of concerns
b_aliases: Madhyamaka -- time-indexed K_t losing a determination not emptiness

group_evidence.why_grouped: labels co-occur in the same contribution's labels[] 3 separate times across the corpus

a_rows_sample.anchor: We now move from system boundary to the inside of the system. Component=Responsibility+Data+Behavior+Interface+Dependency+Evidence. A component is therefore not defined merely by its directory or class name.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines Component=Responsibility+Data+Behavior+Interface+Dependency+Evidence, stating a component is not defined merely by its directory or class name.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.1 — Component reconstruction principle ... C=(Identity,Purpose,Responsibilities,Data,Commands,Queries,Dependencies,Interfaces,Invariants,Tests,Runtime,Owner). Only after these are established can we decide whether two components are separate, overlapping, duplicates, parts of one bounded context
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines the full component reconstruction tuple C=(Identity,Purpose,Responsibilities,Data,Commands,Queries,Dependencies,Interfaces,Invariants,Tests,Runtime,Owner), a precondition for classifying inter-component relationships.

type_signature.codomain: Identity x Purpose x Responsibilities x Data x Commands x Queries x Dependencies x Interfaces x Invariants x Tests x Runtime x Owner

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.2 — First question: what is a component? ... Class, Module, Package, Service, Application, DeploymentUnit, BoundedContext. They are not equivalent.
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes seven frequently-confused units of analysis: Class, Module, Package, Service, Application, DeploymentUnit, BoundedContext.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.3 — Experiment 1 ... Repository contains KnowledgeService.java. Can we conclude KnowledgeService=KnowledgeBoundedContext? No. It may simply be an application service. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 1: a KnowledgeService.java class does not by itself establish a KnowledgeBoundedContext; it may be merely an application service; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.4 — Component levels ... System→BoundedContext→{Application,Domain,Infrastructure}, plus Supporting Systems. This prevents accidental conflation of implementation structure and domain structure.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines a multi-level reconstruction tree (System->BoundedContext->{Application,Domain,Infrastructure}, Supporting Systems) preventing conflation of implementation and domain structure.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.5 — Component identity ... ComponentID should not depend solely on ClassName. Because names change.
a_rows_sample.statement: States component identity must be stable and independent of class naming, since names change.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.6 — Experiment 2 ... Class KnowledgeService becomes EngineeringKnowledgeService. Expected: potentially the same logical component. Result: PASS. This is why logical identity and implementation naming must be separated.
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 2: a renamed class (KnowledgeService to EngineeringKnowledgeService) may remain the same logical component; result PASS, motivating separation of logical identity from naming.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.7 — Responsibility reconstruction ... What responsibility does this component actually own? Not what does its README claim? We inspect Commands+Queries+DataMutations+Dependencies.
a_rows_sample.statement: States responsibility must be reconstructed from actual Commands+Queries+DataMutations+Dependencies, not from README claims.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.8 — Experiment 3 ... Component named KnowledgeManager actually reads Git, parses Markdown, creates embeddings, writes vector data. Expected: observed responsibility closer to KnowledgeIngestion/Indexing than KnowledgeAuthority. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 3: a KnowledgeManager's actual behavior (reads Git, parses Markdown, creates embeddings, writes vector data) reveals its real responsibility as KnowledgeIngestion/Indexing rather than KnowledgeAuthority; result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.9 — Responsibility is more important than naming ... ObservedBehavior > ComponentName for determining actual responsibility.
a_rows_sample.statement: States the central rule ObservedBehavior>ComponentName for determining actual component responsibility.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.10 — Data ownership ... Which data does the component own? We distinguish Reads(Data) from Owns(Data). A service can read data without owning it.
a_rows_sample.statement: Distinguishes Reads(Data) from Owns(Data): a service reading data does not thereby own it.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.11 — Experiment 4 ... Component A reads Decision. Component B creates and changes Decision. Expected: B is the stronger candidate for ownership. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 4: the component that creates and changes Decision (B) is the stronger ownership candidate over one that merely reads it (A); result PASS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.12 — Data ownership graph ... Component-owns->Data and separately Component-reads->Data. This becomes crucial for determining bounded-context boundaries.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines the data-ownership graph with separate owns and reads edge types, crucial for bounded-context boundary determination.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.13 — Experiment 5 ... Two services directly modify the same decision table. Expected: potential shared-data coupling. Result: OBS. This does not yet prove architectural failure, but it is an important finding.
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 5: two services directly mutating the same decision table is potential shared-data coupling, classified OBS (an important finding, not yet a proven failure).

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.14 — Aggregate ownership ... Aggregate→Invariant→Owner. Decision may own invariants such as Approved⇒AuthorityPresent.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines the aggregate-ownership model Aggregate→Invariant→Owner, illustrated by Decision owning Approved⇒AuthorityPresent.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.15 — Experiment 6 ... Two unrelated services can independently set decision.status=APPROVED without passing through a common invariant boundary. Expected: potential aggregate-boundary violation. Result: OBS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 6: two independent services both able to set decision.status=APPROVED without a shared invariant boundary is a potential aggregate-boundary violation, classified OBS.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.16 — Command ownership ... Command→OwningComponent. CreateEvidence, ApproveDecision, RegisterAgent, RecordObservation.
a_rows_sample.statement: Defines command ownership Command→OwningComponent, with example commands CreateEvidence/ApproveDecision/RegisterAgent/RecordObservation.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.17 — Experiment 7 ... Both Service A and Service B implement ApproveDecision. Expected: potential duplicate business responsibility. Result: OBS. This is exactly the kind of issue the actual inventory should expose.
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 7: two services both implementing ApproveDecision is potential duplicate business responsibility, classified OBS, exemplifying the inventory's diagnostic purpose.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.18 — Query ownership ... Query→OwningSource. But multiple read models may legitimately expose the same information. DuplicateReadModel≠DuplicateDomainOwnership.
a_rows_sample.statement: States DuplicateReadModel≠DuplicateDomainOwnership: multiple read models exposing the same information may be legitimate rather than duplicated ownership.

a_rows_sample.anchor: 111.19 — Experiment 8 ... Two APIs expose GET /decisions. One is a UI projection. The other is the authoritative domain API. Expected: not automatically a duplicate domain capability. Result: PASS
a_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 8: a UI-projection GET /decisions endpoint alongside an authoritative domain API endpoint is not automatically duplicate domain capability; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: We now need to establish the actual boundary of KnowledgeOS before analyzing individual components. This distinction is essential because otherwise the architecture will gradually absorb every tool that touches the platform.
b_rows_sample.statement: States the need to establish the actual KnowledgeOS boundary before component analysis, warning that without it the architecture would gradually absorb every tool that touches the platform.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 110.1 — The system boundary rule ... K_OS={x | x has an evidenced architectural role in KnowledgeOS}. Not K_OS={x | x happens to interact with KnowledgeOS}. An external Git server may be essential to KnowledgeOS without becoming part of KnowledgeOS itself.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines K_OS={x | x has an evidenced architectural role in KnowledgeOS}, explicitly rejecting the weaker K_OS={x | x happens to interact with KnowledgeOS}.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 110.2 — Six boundary classifications ... CORE, SUPPORTING, AGENT, EXTERNAL, LEGACY, UNKNOWN. This is intentionally conservative.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines six intentionally conservative boundary classifications: CORE, SUPPORTING, AGENT, EXTERNAL, LEGACY, UNKNOWN.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 110.3 — CORE ... A component is CORE when removing it would remove an essential KnowledgeOS capability. Examples: KnowledgeModel, KnowledgePersistence, GovernanceEngine, EvidenceModel, if these actually exist in the implementation. But we must verify their existence.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines CORE as a component whose removal would remove an essential capability, listing candidate examples pending verification of actual existence.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 110.4 — SUPPORTING ... Database, MessageBroker, ObjectStorage, CI/CD, Observability. Used by KnowledgeOS does not mean semantically part of KnowledgeOS.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines SUPPORTING infrastructure (Database/MessageBroker/ObjectStorage/CI-CD/Observability), stating usage does not entail semantic membership.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 110.5 — AGENT ... .claude/, .codex/, AGENTS.md, agent hooks, agent commands, agent-specific settings. Their purpose is AgentBehavior. They become part of the broader ecosystem but should not automatically be classified as the KnowledgeOS semantic core.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines AGENT classification for .claude/.codex/AGENTS.md and agent hooks/commands/settings, ecosystem members not automatically semantic core.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 110.6 — EXTERNAL ... GitHub, GitLab, Jira, CI, CloudProvider. Its data may become KnowledgeOS evidence, but the external system retains its own system boundary.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines EXTERNAL systems (GitHub/GitLab/Jira/CI/CloudProvider) that retain their own boundary even as their data becomes KnowledgeOS evidence.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 110.7 — LEGACY ... old-memory-sync, old-registry, deprecated-indexer, legacy-agent-script. A repository containing an artifact does not mean the artifact belongs to the current architecture.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines LEGACY artifacts as especially dangerous for creating false architectural impressions, since repository presence does not entail current-architecture membership.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 110.8 — UNKNOWN ... This is a legitimate result. It means we have not yet established enough evidence to classify the artifact. It does not mean External.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines UNKNOWN as a legitimate classification meaning insufficient evidence, explicitly distinct from External.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 110.9 — Experiment 1 ... scripts/session-changes-logger. Is it Core, Supporting, Agent, External or Legacy? If invoked by agent hooks: likely AGENT/SUPPORTING. But classification awaits evidence. Result: UNKNOWN until usage is established
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 1: session-changes-logger's classification (likely AGENT/SUPPORTING if hook-invoked) is UNKNOWN until usage evidence is established.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 110.10 — Experiment 2 ... .claude/settings.json controls Claude execution. Expected: AGENT. It is not automatically CORE KnowledgeOS. Result: AGENT
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 2: .claude/settings.json is classified AGENT, not automatically CORE KnowledgeOS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 110.11 — Experiment 3 ... A PostgreSQL database stores KnowledgeOS records. Expected: SUPPORTING unless the architecture explicitly defines the database as part of the deployable KnowledgeOS product boundary. Result: SUPPORTING
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 3: a PostgreSQL database storing KnowledgeOS records is SUPPORTING unless explicitly defined as part of the deployable product boundary.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 110.12 — Logical boundary versus deployment boundary ... A system may logically contain KnowledgeService while deployment uses PostgreSQL as an external managed service. LogicalBoundary≠DeploymentBoundary.
b_rows_sample.statement: States LogicalBoundary≠DeploymentBoundary: a logical component may be deployed via an externally managed service.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 110.13 — Product boundary versus ecosystem boundary ... Product boundary K_product, Ecosystem boundary K_ecosystem, External environment K_environment. K_product⊆K_ecosystem⊆K_environment.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines a three-tier boundary containment K_product⊆K_ecosystem⊆K_environment (Product/Ecosystem/External-environment boundaries).

b_rows_sample.anchor: 110.14 — Example ... KnowledgeOS Ecosystem diagram: Core (Knowledge/Governance/Assurance), Claude/Codex/CI-CD agents, then GitHub/Jira/Cloud-Infra outer systems interacting without becoming core.
b_rows_sample.statement: Presents a worked ecosystem diagram: KnowledgeOS Core surrounded by Claude/Codex/CI-CD, interacting with outer GitHub/Jira/Cloud-Infra systems without becoming core.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 110.15 — Agent harness boundary ... This resolves an earlier architectural question. Claude and Codex are EcosystemParticipants. Their harnesses are AgentOperatingLayers. KnowledgeOS remains SemanticKnowledge+Governance+Evidence+Assurance according to the actual implementation.
b_rows_sample.statement: Resolves the recurring agent-harness classification question: Claude/Codex are EcosystemParticipants with AgentOperatingLayers, while KnowledgeOS itself is SemanticKnowledge+Governance+Evidence+Assurance.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 110.16 — Experiment 4 ... Codex reads KnowledgeOS architecture. Does that make Codex part of KnowledgeOS? Not necessarily. Expected: Codex=EcosystemParticipant. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 4: Codex reading KnowledgeOS architecture does not make it part of KnowledgeOS; it is classified EcosystemParticipant; result PASS.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 110.17 — But the relationship must be explicit ... Codex-consumes->KnowledgeOS. And potentially Codex-produces->Evidence. This is more informative than simply placing Codex inside the same directory.
b_rows_sample.statement: States the Codex-KnowledgeOS relationship should be modeled explicitly (consumes/produces), more informative than mere directory co-location.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 110.18 — External knowledge sources ... Git, Jira, Confluence, documents, runtime systems. These should be modeled as KnowledgeSources. Not automatically as KnowledgeOS components.
b_rows_sample.statement: Defines external ingestion sources (Git/Jira/Confluence/documents/runtime systems) as KnowledgeSources, not automatically KnowledgeOS components.

b_rows_sample.anchor: 110.19 — Experiment 5 ... Jira contains a change ticket. KnowledgeOS imports it as evidence. Expected: Jira=EXTERNAL, JiraTicket=ExternalEvidenceSource. Result: PASS
b_rows_sample.statement: Experiment 5: an imported Jira ticket is classified Jira=EXTERNAL, JiraTicket=ExternalEvidenceSource; result PASS.
